summary: An applicability statement discussing where the Next Hop Resolution Protocol fits when routing IP over non-broadcast multi-access networks like ATM, SMDS and X.25. It was required by the routing protocol criteria of the time.

eli5.summary: A note saying where and when a certain path-finding tool is a good fit and where it is not.

subtitle: When the Next Hop Resolution Protocol is a good fit for IP over ATM, SMDS and X.25, and where it can go wrong.

tldr.problem: On a large non-broadcast network such as ATM, packets between two hosts in different logical IP subnets are forced through extra routers even though the hosts could reach each other directly.
tldr.mechanism: The Next Hop Resolution Protocol (NHRP) lets a source ask for the NBMA address of the destination, or of the egress router towards it, so it can set up a short-cut. This memo explains the environments where that works well, its scaling limits and its router-to-router loop risk.
tldr.outcome: NHRP does not replace routing. It shortens a path that IP routing already chose, and it needs care when routers use it with each other.

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: IP over NBMA networks such as ATM, SMDS and X.25

facts.label: Safe router-router case
facts.value: Destination adjacent to the egress router's non-NBMA interface

today: RFC 2333 is a Proposed Standard from April 1998 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes where NHRP, defined in RFC 2332, applies.

sections.title: Why an Applicability Statement
sections.content:
The Routing Protocol Criteria in RFC 1264 require a routing protocol to come with a statement of where it applies. RFC 2333 is that statement for the Next Hop Resolution Protocol (NHRP), which is defined in RFC 2332. It covers routing IP datagrams over Non-Broadcast Multiple Access (NBMA) networks such as ATM, SMDS and X.25.

The memo describes NHRP as a generalization of Classical IP and ARP over ATM (RFC 2225) and of IP over SMDS (RFC 1209). It also notes that the ATM Forum decided to adopt and integrate NHRP into its Multiprotocol Over ATM (MPOA) specification.
sections.eli5: Some tools come with a note that says where they work best. This is that note for NHRP, a tool for finding shortcuts across big shared networks.

sections.title: Key Features of NHRP
sections.content:
NHRP generalizes the older schemes in two directions. First, it avoids extra router hops when the source and destination are in different Logical Internet Subnets (LIS) of the same logical NBMA network. Those older specifications make the source send packets to a router that belongs to several LISs. NHRP instead gives the source an inter-LIS address resolution, after which both stations can exchange packets without intermediate routers. This is called short-cut routing.

Second, NHRP is not tied to one NBMA technology, and it was designed to be extensible to network layer protocols other than IP.

If the destination is not attached to the NBMA network, NHRP returns the NBMA address of an exit router with connectivity to it. When NHRP uses dynamic routing to find that router, the answer reflects the routing protocol's choice, which often means the fewest hops.

NHRP is a client-server interaction. A Client issues an NHRP Request. A Server answers it or forwards it to another Server. One entity can be both.

NHRP is not a routing protocol, though it may make use of routing information. It is defined for packets with a single destination and is not intended for direct use in point-to-multipoint communication.
sections.eli5: Normally your message goes through a middle helper even if your friend is close. NHRP tells you your friend's real address so you can deliver it yourself. You ask a helper, and helpers can pass your question along.

sections.title: When to Use a Short-Cut
sections.content:
Issuing an NHRP request is an application dependent decision. A short-cut can have a cost, either money or extra strain on equipment, so a short-lived application with no particular QoS needs may be better served by ordinary hop-by-hop routing. On an NBMA network the key choice becomes short-cut versus hop-by-hop routing, with the application's QoS requirements as the criterion, rather than the old question of local versus remote.

To avoid several short-cuts being formed for the same packet, the memo suggests that only these entities issue an NHRP request:

  • the host that originates the IP packet, if it has an NBMA interface;
  • the first router along the path whose next hop is reachable through its NBMA interface;
  • a policy router within the NBMA network that the packet has to traverse.

Short-cuts also let features of the NBMA network be used end to end. For ATM, QoS guarantees can be used without re-assembling and re-segmenting IP packets at each network layer hop.
sections.eli5: A shortcut is not always worth it. If you are only passing a quick note, the normal route is fine. Only the person who starts the message, or the first helper near the big network, should ask for the shortcut, so you do not end up with many.

sections.title: Routers, Loops and Changing Routes
sections.content:
NHRP works for host-host, host-router and router-host communication. When used router-router, NHRP as defined in RFC 2332 can produce persistent routing loops if the underlying routing protocol loses information critical to loop suppression. This can happen when router metrics change across autonomous system boundaries. A separate document was to address loop-free router-router use.

One case is safe: the destination host is directly adjacent to the non-NBMA interface of the egress router, in a stable configuration. If a Request has the Q bit set, which shows the requester is a router, and the destination is not adjacent, the egress router can safely send a negative reply (NAK). That forces the data packets to follow the routed path.

Frequent route changes, on a scale of seconds, also hurt. They can cause loops in some router-router cases, and in host-router cases they can cause short-cut paths to be created over and over and then live only briefly.
sections.eli5: If two helpers both think the other knows a shortcut, a message can go round in circles. So a helper that is not sure should just say no and let the message take the normal road. Also, if the roads keep changing, building shortcuts is a waste.

sections.title: Scalability at Three Levels
sections.content:
The memo looks at scale for unicast traffic at the client, LIS and domain levels.

  • Client level: the processing and memory of the NIC that connects to the NBMA network can be the limit. A router may need a large number of SVCCs out of its NBMA interface because it aggregates traffic from many sources.
  • LIS level: a large LIS must store and serve many NBMA to network layer address mappings. NHRP can use the Server Cache Synchronization Protocol (SCSP, RFC 2334) to keep several NHSs in a LIS synchronized.
  • Domain level: resolving a destination outside the LIS relies on network layer routing, so NHRP scales in the same order as the routing algorithm, provided all routers on the path are NHRP aware.

A router that does not implement NHRP silently discards a Request, and then connectivity is hop-by-hop. With dynamic routing, virtually all routers in the logical NBMA network should therefore be NHRP aware. Static routing needs fewer NHRP routers, since the manually defined paths name them, but static routing does not scale, can give persistently suboptimal routes off the NBMA network, and has fairly negative failure modes.
sections.eli5: A shortcut system can get too busy at three places: the single computer's network card, the helpers in one neighbourhood, and the whole city. Helpers that team up share the load. And every helper along the way has to know the trick, or the message just takes the long way.

sections.title: How NHRP Relates to Routing
sections.content: NHRP does not replace existing routing protocols. Routing decides the path. If that path goes out through an NBMA interface, NHRP may be used there to resolve the destination IP address into an NBMA address. Packets are then forwarded using the forwarding and path determination of the NBMA network itself. In other words, NHRP creates a short-cut track on a path that IP routing had already determined, and so it shortens the routed path.
sections.eli5: The map still tells you which way to go. NHRP only checks whether there is a quicker door along that same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: NHRP is an address resolution protocol and SCSP is a database synchronization protocol, so both may face spoofing (of a server for NHRP, of a peer for SCSP) and denial of service attacks. Both provide authentication mechanisms for environments where spoofing is a concern. The memo raises no further security concerns beyond those in the referenced sections of RFC 2332 and RFC 2334.
sections.eli5: Someone could pretend to be a helper and give wrong directions. Both tools have a password-style check to stop that.
